narrative:
The model has analyzed your academic situation and determined that there’s a **19% chance** you might not pass your final year. While this isn’t a certainty, it’s high enough that the school has decided you should take extra support courses to help you succeed. Think of it like a warning sign—just as you’d pay attention if your car’s check engine light came on, this is the system’s way of saying, *"Let’s give you a boost before things get harder."*

The biggest factors pushing this prediction are three key areas. First, the **reason you chose this school** stands out as the strongest influence working *in your favor*—meaning it actually lowers the risk of failing. Most students attend for the course quality or because it’s close to home, but you picked it for its reputation, which suggests you’re motivated by high standards. That’s a positive sign, but it’s not enough on its own.

The second factor is your **history of past failures**. Unlike most students who’ve never failed a class, you haven’t had any—this is another strong positive. It shows you’ve been keeping up so far, which is great, but the model is still flagging concerns because of other areas.

The third factor is your **goal to pursue higher education**. Almost every student says they want to go on to university, so this doesn’t set you apart in a negative way. However, it does mean the stakes feel higher: the system is treating this as a critical moment to make sure you’re on track for those future plans.

The real red flags come from other parts of your profile. For example, you’ve missed **10 school days**—far more than the average student, which disrupts your learning. Your **health is currently very poor**, and your **free time after school is extremely high**, meaning you might not be balancing study and rest well. While you *do* have family support and internet access at home, these positives aren’t enough to offset the risks tied to your health, absences, and study habits.

Here’s what you should do next: **Focus on reducing your absences**—even small improvements here can make a big difference. Use your family’s support to create a study schedule that fits your health needs, and consider cutting back on time spent going out if it’s interfering with your focus. The remedial courses are there to help, so treat them as a chance to strengthen the areas where you’re most at risk. You’ve got this—small steps now can turn that 19% into a confident success.
